lines.text: and its dwellings, gardens and landscape! When we really
take to our hearts the beauty of the morning sunlight, we
can begin our day's work with renewed joy and vigour.
How many a morning of course steals upon us, grey with
cloud and mist! And it is not always easy for us to assimilate
the blessing of the new day. But how desirable it would be
if we could do so always with a moment of silent meditation,
a prayer or a hymn, whether alone or in fellowship with the
other members of our family. It would be so salutary for our
mood during the day's work, for the way in which we
approach the people with whom we have dealings, if only
each day began with quiet self-recollection in the presence
of God, with thanksgiving and petition. How often do we
begin the day quite thoughtlessly, and hardly have we
awakened from sleep when we are again caught up in the
cares and the business of life. We can see from the behaviour
of people how they have begun their day; many a popular
expression brings home the same truth. But even when we
have had a time of quiet and prayer in the early morning,
how often it is quickly forgotten in the bustle of the new day!
How grateful we should be for Sunday which brings an
interruption to the work of the week, which stands out as a
day of rest from the agitation and tumult of our week's work,
which invites us to pause and reflect in God's presence, when
the bells ring out with their appeal: "Come to me, all who
labour and are heavy laden."
Are we not all weary and heavy laden? Laden with the
burdens of the week, and the grime of everyday toil? What a
load of trouble and care each week brings, what petty and
exhausting tasks, oftentimes frustrating labour! And this is
the case even when we are engaged in work which delights
us and expresses our sense of personal vocation. Even the
most fruitful labour is in the long run undermining and
fatiguing, and we notice this at the end of the week. And we
notice it still more if at any time we have spent a Sunday
without due rest, whether from frivolous motives, or because
on Sunday there was so much to get done which in the week
we had to set aside.
